studies.title: Yet They Say He Made It Up
studies.meaning: Three disconnected letters open the surah, and then a flat declaration: this Book comes down from the Lord of the Worlds, and no doubt attaches to it. The third ayah quotes the objection before anyone raises it, that a man invented this, and answers it by restating the claim rather than arguing for it. The purpose given is narrow: to warn a people no warner had reached. Guidance is then named as the hoped-for result, not the guaranteed one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stretch of the mission when the charge of authorship was being made publicly and often. The commentators attach no particular occasion to these ayat and read them as part of the running Meccan dispute over where the recitation came from. The people described as having received no warner before are generally understood to be the Arabs of that region, who had no prophet in living memory.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun on a pattern that implies gradual, staged descent rather than one delivery. The manner of the revelation, given in portions across years, is folded into the claim about its source.
Stronger than ordinary uncertainty. It names a suspicion that disturbs and refuses to settle, so what the ayah denies is not just intellectual hesitation but the restlessness that comes with it.
From a root for cutting and stitching leather into a shape. The accusation is one of assembly, taking material that exists and working it into something new, rather than of invention from nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on the reliability of transmitted speech. Poetry, genealogies and the terms of treaties were carried in memory and recited back in public, and a man's standing depended on whether his words held up when others repeated them. To accuse someone of making up what he attributed to another was the most serious charge available in that setting, and here it was aimed at a man his accusers had known since childhood.
studies.didYouKnow: The letters that open this surah begin exactly six surahs of the Quran: this one and surahs two, three, twenty-nine, thirty and thirty-one. At thirty ayat this is much the shortest of the six, against the two hundred and eighty-six of the longest. The classical commentators record several readings of the disconnected letters and decline to settle between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is placed in the Book's origin rather than in its contents, which reverses the order a modern reader expects. A limit is also set on what a warner accomplishes: he warns, and guidance may follow. The closing particle leaves that outcome genuinely open, so prophecy is described as an errand with a purpose rather than a mechanism that produces belief in whoever hears it.

crossReferences.why: Meets the same charge of fabrication by pointing at the Book's confirmation of the scriptures before it.
Answers the accusation by inviting the objectors to produce ten comparable surahs of their own.
Repeats the reason given here, to warn a people whose fathers were not warned.

studies.applyIt: The next time you open the Quran, notice where your attention goes: to what the words say, or to whether you trust where they came from. This passage puts the second question first and answers it before saying anything else. Try one sitting this week in that order, source before content, and see whether the sentences land differently.

studies.title: Six Days, Then The Throne
studies.meaning: Creation is given a duration, six days, followed by a settling upon the Throne, and the ayah moves straight from that to a consequence for the listener: apart from Him you have no protector and no intercessor. The classical commentators treat the days as periods whose length is not disclosed, and they affirm the settling without describing it. The closing question is not decoration. It is the destination the two earlier clauses were built to reach.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience already granted that God had made the heavens and the earth; what they disputed was whether He alone should be approached. The ayah takes the agreed premise and draws the contested conclusion from it. Commentators note that intercession was the working assumption of religious practice in Mecca, where lesser figures were addressed in the expectation that a request would be carried upward on the petitioner's behalf.

keyTerms.note: The classical commentators affirm the word as revealed and decline to say how, holding that it states a relation of sovereignty over the Throne without licensing any picture of place or posture.
From a root meaning to make even, to join a second to something single. An intercessor pairs his standing with yours, and the ayah denies that anyone stands available to be paired in this way.
A reflexive form built on remembering. It asks not for new information but for retrieval of something already held, which is why the question follows a premise the listeners had never denied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca held images that pilgrims addressed as go-betweens, and the vocabulary of intercession was the vocabulary of ordinary life. A man in debt or in danger found someone with standing to speak for him to a chief. Protection was brokered rather than asked for directly, and everyone knew the going rate in obligation. This ayah cuts across the habit at its root, by removing the broker instead of arguing over which broker to choose.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as six days occurs seven times in the Quran, in surahs seven, ten, eleven, twenty-five, this one, fifty and fifty-seven. In each place it is joined to a further statement, and the further statements are all different: a throne, a testing of deeds, a denial that any fatigue was involved, a claim about what God knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting sovereignty and the absence of intercession in a single breath makes access to God a consequence of His having made everything. Nothing in creation stands outside the making, so nothing can stand between. The verb for taking heed also implies the listener already holds what he needs to reach this conclusion, which lets unbelief be described as a failure of recollection rather than a shortage of evidence.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit on intercession inside the best-known description of God's sovereignty.
Gives the six days and the Throne, then adds the night and day as running evidence.
Places intercession wholly with God, answering the assumption this ayah removes.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you asked someone to put in a word for you, and how differently you spoke to that person than you would have spoken to the one deciding. Notice the shift. Then pray tonight without any of that middle language, no arranging of your case, and see what is left when there is nobody to persuade.

studies.title: The Affair Ascends To Him
studies.meaning: Between the settling on the Throne and the knowledge of the unseen, this ayah describes traffic. The affair is directed downward from heaven to earth and then climbs back. Commentators read the descent as the ordering of events and commands and the ascent as their return for reckoning. The day named at the close is measured rather than described, a thousand years by human counting, and the classical readings differ over what exactly that figure measures.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a surah arguing that the God who made the world also runs it and will call it to account. The ayah addresses a specific gap: the Meccans acknowledged a creator but did not attribute the ongoing government of events to Him in daily practice. No occasion is reported for it. Commentators read it as a link in the surah's argument, moving from creation towards judgement.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for the back or rear of a thing, and so for its outcome. To manage in this sense is to arrange something with its end already in view, which is where the surah is heading.
A verb of stepped rising rather than instant transfer. The same root names the ways of ascent in another surah, and it gives the returning affair both a path and a duration.
A noun of measurement from the root for determining and apportioning. It presents the day as a quantity that can be set against human counting, not as an image of time without limit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A thousand years was no abstraction to people who traced descent through named ancestors and dated a well or a truce by generations. Caravans measured distance in days of travel; a message carried to Syria and answered could take most of a season. Everyone present knew the weight of a day as a unit of waiting. The ayah takes that unit and stretches it past anything a merchant's reckoning could hold.
studies.didYouKnow: The measure of a thousand years appears once more in the Quran with the same sense, where a day with your Lord is said to be like a thousand years of what you count. A third passage names a different figure, fifty thousand years. The classical commentators generally read the two as descriptions of different days rather than as a discrepancy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah adds government to creation. A maker who withdraws once the making is finished is a familiar enough idea, and this sentence closes it off by describing continuous movement of command downward and return upward. The measured day then sets human time inside a larger scale without abolishing it. A thousand years is still a number, which keeps the hereafter continuous with experience rather than wholly other.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same thousand-year measure while answering those who demanded the punishment come quickly.
Names a day of fifty thousand years, the passage classical commentators set beside this one.
Asks directly who it is that directs the affair, and lets the objectors answer.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are currently waiting on and write down how long you have been waiting, in weeks. Then read this ayah again with that number in mind. The point is not to feel small about it. It is to notice that the waiting has a shape and an upward direction, and that you have been measuring only the near end of it.

studies.title: From Clay And From Water
studies.meaning: Three statements carry the human being into existence. Everything God made, He made well. The first origination was from clay. The continuation was from an extract of a fluid the passage calls lowly. Commentators read the sequence as covering both the first making and every making since. It is deliberately unflattering about the material and openly admiring of the workmanship, and it holds those two judgements together instead of choosing one, which is the whole point of the order.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to listeners who denied that a body once decayed could be reassembled. The surah has established God's sovereignty and now turns to the listener's own origin as the nearest available evidence. Commentators read the passage as an argument rather than as description: what was begun from clay and is continued from a drop cannot be beyond a second making by the same hand.

keyTerms.note: The verb for doing something beautifully rather than merely correctly. Applied to everything created, it makes fitness for purpose, not appearance, the standard by which the making is being praised.
A noun for what is gently pulled out of something larger, the way a blade is drawn from its sheath. It occurs only twice in the Quran, both times inside an account of how a human being is made.
From a root for weakness and contempt. The judgement falls on the substance rather than on the person, which is what lets the next ayah speak of a spirit breathed into it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clay was the working material of settled life in and beyond Mecca: cooking pots, ovens, the walls and floors of houses in the oases. Potters were an ordinary sight, and everyone knew a shaped vessel began as mud and would slump back into it if the firing went wrong. To hear that a human being was begun from clay was to hear a claim in the vocabulary of daily handling rather than of myth.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for an extract occurs only twice in the Quran, here and in a longer account of the stages of the embryo. The phrase for the lowly fluid also occurs exactly twice, here and in a short surah that turns it into a question about God's power. Both of those other passages sit inside arguments about the second creation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worth is assigned twice, in opposite directions, and neither assignment cancels the other. The material is called lowly; the workmanship is called excellent. Human dignity in this passage is therefore not a property of the substance a person is made from but of the care taken over the making, which is how the same surah can describe the body as an extract of fluid and still treat the person as answerable.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the stages of the same extract at greater length and closes on a blessing.
Repeats the phrase for the lowly fluid inside a question about what God is able to do.
Traces the same arc from dust and a drop through old age to an appointed term.

studies.applyIt: Hold your own hand in front of you for a moment and consider that this passage would describe it with two words at once, lowly and well made. Most people can manage only one of those about themselves at a time. Try holding both this evening, without resolving the tension, and notice which one you keep reaching to drop.

studies.title: Rarely Do You Give Thanks
studies.meaning: The forming of a person is completed by two acts, a proportioning and a breathing of spirit, and the sentence then turns without pause to a list of instruments: hearing, eyesight, hearts. The closing clause is not a general complaint about ingratitude. It is about these three in particular. Commentators note that the grammar shifts here from speaking about humanity to speaking to the listener, so the argument stops being anthropology and becomes an address.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's account of how a person is assembled. The three faculties named recur across the Meccan surahs as standing evidence in arguments about accountability, since they are the means by which any message can be received at all. No occasion is reported for the ayah. Commentators read the change into direct address as the moment the argument turns on the person hearing it.

keyTerms.note: A verb of making even and bringing into balance. It describes not the assembly of parts but their adjustment to one another, the finishing that turns collected material into a working whole.

The classical commentators read the attachment to God as one of honour rather than of division, and they record that the nature of the spirit is among the things the Quran deliberately declines to explain.
A plural used of the heart as the seat of understanding rather than of feeling. Placed after hearing and sight, it names the faculty that does something with what those two bring in.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society that carried its literature in memory, hearing was the primary organ of learning. A poem was heard once, held, and repeated years later; a contract was witnessed by ear and enforced on that basis. Sight belonged to the road and the herd, to reading weather, tracks and the horizon. The three faculties listed here were the entire apparatus of a working life, so naming them together named everything a person had.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a breathing of God's spirit occurs five times in the Quran. Twice it belongs to the making of Adam, twice to the conception of Jesus, and once here, where it is said of the human being in general. That is why the classical commentators read this ayah as describing every person rather than one moment at the beginning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accountability is grounded in equipment. A creature given the means to hear, see and understand is by that fact answerable for what it does with them, and the closing clause treats thanks as the natural use of a faculty rather than an extra duty laid on top. The proportioning also implies human beings are not defective by design; whatever goes wrong later is not traced here to the making.

crossReferences.why: Names the same faculties as what God gave when you knew nothing, and ends on thanks.
Says the same three will each be questioned, turning the gift into a reckoning.
Uses the same two verbs, proportioning and breathing, of the making of Adam.

studies.applyIt: Choose one of the three today and use it deliberately once. Listen to somebody for two minutes without preparing your reply. Or look at one ordinary thing long enough to see something you had not noticed in it. Thanks in this ayah is not a phrase you add afterwards; it is the faculty being used for what it is for.

studies.title: The Angel Put In Charge
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted in the objectors' own words: once we are lost in the earth, are we really to be made new. The reply does not argue about bodies. It names an agent, an angel of death assigned to you, and then states the destination. Commentators observe that the answer changes the subject from mechanism to authority, and that the last clause of the first ayah identifies the real difficulty as unwillingness to meet God rather than trouble with physics.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the long argument over resurrection that runs through the surahs of this period. The objection quoted here was a live one and appears in several forms across the Quran, sometimes as a taunt and sometimes as a genuine question. Commentators attach no named occasion to these two ayat, reading them as a representative exchange rather than the record of one conversation in Mecca.

keyTerms.note: Ordinarily the verb for losing a road or a stray camel. Applied to a body in the ground it pictures scattering into something larger until the parts can no longer be told apart from it.
From a root for paying a debt completely, with nothing withheld. Death is presented as a collection of what is owed rather than as a destruction, so nothing is treated as lost in the taking.
A passive form from the word for delegation. The angel is a deputy rather than a power over death in his own right, which places the whole event under the authority named at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in that country was quick and shallow, in stony ground at the edge of settlement, and the dryness did the rest. People had seen old graves opened by flood or wind and knew precisely what was left. The objection in these ayat is not the scepticism of a philosopher. It is the report of men who had looked into the ground and drawn what seemed to them the only available conclusion.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for the angel of death occurs once in the whole Quran, here. Elsewhere the taking of souls is attributed to God directly, or to angels in the plural who are described as messengers. The classical commentators record the variation and read the accounts as complementary rather than as competing descriptions of one event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a question about matter with a statement about agency moves the resurrection out of the category of natural possibility and into the category of appointment. Death becomes something performed on a person rather than something that merely happens to a body, and the passive verb keeps the angel from turning into an independent power. What the objectors were really denying is finally named, and it is not a process but a meeting.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same objection about decayed bones by pointing back at the first creation.
Describes messengers who take the soul at death, the plural account alongside this singular one.
Attributes the taking of souls to God directly, and includes what happens in sleep.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this passage answers a question about how with an answer about who. You probably have a worry shaped the same way, where you keep asking how something could possibly work out. Try restating it once today as a question about who is handling it. Not as consolation, but to see whether the original question was the one you actually needed answered.

studies.title: The Request To Be Returned
studies.meaning: The scene is given as an unfinished sentence, if only you could see them, and what would be seen is posture before it is speech: heads hanging. Their words then claim the two things they had denied, that they have seen and have heard, and ask for a return in order to act. The commentators read the request as sincere and useless at the same time. Certainty arrives, and the ayah lets it arrive exactly where it can no longer be spent on anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just quoted these same objectors denying the meeting with their Lord, and here they are shown on the far side of it. Commentators treat the passage as a scene of the Day of Resurrection rather than a report of any occasion, and note that the Quran stages this request repeatedly, in different mouths, as the characteristic speech of that day.

keyTerms.note: Used of a head turned downward and of anything reversed from its natural position. The word carries the physical droop and the inversion of a former posture at once, which is why it comes before the speech.
The verb of perceiving rather than of merely looking at. Set before hearing, it reverses the order this surah used earlier and marks that what had been asserted is now under their own eyes.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and no longer wavers. It is the word used of the believers' certainty in this life, and here the identical state arrives too late to count for anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The gesture described was legible to everyone. A man brought before a chief with his case already lost stood with his head down; a captive led in from a raid was walked in the same posture. Public life was conducted face to face in small assemblies, and the tilt of a head settled a question before anyone spoke. The ayah relies on that shared reading of bodies instead of describing an emotion.
studies.didYouKnow: The request to be sent back appears in several passages of the Quran, in the singular and the plural, and it is refused every time. In one place the refusal is immediate and a barrier is described behind the speaker. The classical commentators treat the recurrence as deliberate patterning across the Book rather than as a set of separate episodes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes its point about the timing of belief rather than its content. What these speakers say is entirely correct. It is simply said in a place where saying it costs nothing and risks nothing. Faith in this life is therefore defined partly by the exposure of possibly being wrong, and the ayah shows what conviction is worth once that exposure has been removed from it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same request in one man's voice and answers it with an immediate refusal.
Shows the same wish voiced at the Fire, and says what they would do if granted.
Records the plea to be brought out to act righteously, along with the answer given.

studies.applyIt: There is probably something you have decided you will deal with once you are sure. Notice that this ayah is about people who finally became sure. Take the smallest version of that thing today and do it while the doubt is still there. Not because doubt does not matter, but because acting is only available on this side of certainty.

studies.title: The Guidance Not Imposed
studies.meaning: A power is conceded and then said not to have been used. God could have given every soul its guidance; instead a word already spoken will be made good. The commentators handle the sentence with care. It establishes that guidance lies within God's power without turning anyone's refusal into something done to them, since the surah has just shown these speakers turning away with every faculty intact. The two halves are held side by side rather than reconciled.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed directly after the scene in which the guilty ask to be returned. Their request has been left hanging, and this ayah supplies the reason no such return will be arranged. Commentators connect the declaration referred to here with the word spoken at the beginning of the human story, when the first refusal was answered. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah itself.

keyTerms.note: A verb of effective will, whose object comes about simply by being willed. Setting it inside a sentence about what did not happen is what makes the ayah a statement of restraint rather than of power.
From the root for truth and for a right that has to be paid. The declaration is not merely accurate; it is owed, which is why the outcome is presented as a settlement rather than a decision.
The definite article points back to something already said rather than introducing it here. Commentators read it as the word spoken at the opening of the human story about who would fill the Fire.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A word given in that society functioned as a kind of property. Oaths bound clans for generations, and a chief who failed to make good on a stated intention lost the standing everything else rested on. Debts of honour outlived the men who incurred them. To say that a word will come true was therefore to speak in the strongest register available for guaranteeing that a stated future would actually arrive.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this contrary-to-fact construction, had We willed We could have, in a number of places, and what goes undone is almost always something overwhelming: a sign that would leave every neck bowed, a single undivided community, guidance given to everyone on earth. The pattern describes God's power precisely by listing what that power has declined to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to simplify the human situation in either direction. It does not say people are simply free while God stands back, and it does not say they are compelled. It says universal guidance was possible and was not given, and locates the reason in a prior word rather than in anyone's merit. The classical tradition treats this pairing as a boundary on speculation rather than a puzzle awaiting solution.

crossReferences.why: Says the same of belief, that everyone on earth would have believed had God willed it.
Repeats that one community was possible, then states the same word about filling Hell.
Grants that a compelling sign could be sent down, and says it was not.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you explain another person's refusal to yourself by deciding what kind of person they must be. This ayah declines to do that about anyone, even here. For one conversation this week, hold the verdict about what someone is and stay with what they actually said. You will find the second thing much harder to keep hold of.

studies.title: Because You Forgot This Day
studies.meaning: The sentence is built on one verb used twice, and the second use is answering the first. What is charged is not disbelief in the abstract but forgetting a meeting, letting a known appointment slide out of view. The reply uses the same word back. The commentators are careful here: forgetting is impossible for God, so they read the second use as a matched response, being left where you placed yourself, phrased in the language of the charge rather than describing a lapse.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to those who had just asked to be returned and act righteously. This is the answer that follows the refusal. The surah has been arguing from creation and government towards a reckoning, and here the reckoning is stated in the second person for the first time. Commentators report no particular occasion, reading the ayah as the conclusion of the scene that opened three ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: The verb of tasting rather than of suffering, repeated twice in this one ayah. It names direct first-hand contact with something previously known only as a report, which is exactly what these speakers had refused.

The Arabic covers both losing something from memory and deliberately setting it aside. The second sense carries the weight here, since what is described is a choice to stop attending rather than an accident.
A noun of remaining rather than an adjective, so the ayah names duration itself rather than describing the torment as long. The same root supplies the word used of the gardens elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Abandonment was the sharpest sanction that world knew. A man cast out of his clan's protection had no standing at all: his blood could be spilled without consequence and no one would speak for him in an assembly. Being forgotten was not an emotional injury but a legal condition. The listeners would have heard the second half of this ayah as the withdrawal of protection, in the exact terms they used among themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrasing in which God says that a people are forgotten as they forgot occurs in only a handful of places in the Quran, and the exact form used here is not repeated. The classical commentators discuss it at length and agree the wording is deliberately reciprocal, mirroring the charge back rather than attributing forgetfulness to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats attention as a moral category. What is punished is not an argument lost but an appointment allowed to fade, which makes ordinary distraction a serious matter rather than a small one. The mirrored verb also shows how the Quran describes recompense: not as an unrelated penalty attached to an offence, but as the offence itself handed back with nothing softening it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the reciprocal wording almost exactly, addressed to those who forgot this meeting.
Answers a complaint about blindness with the same pattern: you forgot, so you are forgotten.
Turns the mirror inward: those who forgot God were made to forget their own selves.

studies.applyIt: Think of one commitment you have not broken but have simply stopped thinking about. Not a duty someone is chasing you for, but something you decided once and let go quiet. Write it on a piece of paper today and put it where you will see it tomorrow morning. This ayah is about the distance between denying something and letting it fall out of view.

studies.title: They Fall Down Prostrate
studies.meaning: Belief is defined here by what a body does when a reminder arrives. The construction is exclusive, so the ayah is drawing a boundary rather than praising a group: these are the ones who believe in Our signs. Three things are named in order, a falling into prostration, a glorifying joined to praise, and the absence of pride. The commentators note that the last item is stated negatively, as something not done, which makes it the condition the other two rest on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, arriving directly after a scene of the Fire and the refusal of a request to return. The surah turns from those who let the reminder pass to those in whom it lands, and describes them by their response rather than by their affiliation. Commentators report no specific occasion. The contrast with the preceding ayat is the context the passage is written to supply.

keyTerms.note: A verb of falling rather than of lowering oneself deliberately. It implies weight giving way, so the ayah describes a response arriving faster than the decision to make it would.
An intensive plural of the participle, describing the posture as a condition they are in rather than an action they perform. The surah takes its name from this word and from what it names.
A form that means seeking greatness for oneself rather than possessing it. What is denied is the claim, not the stature, which is why the negation can stand as a description of character.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Putting the face to the ground was a strong gesture in a culture that guarded standing carefully. Free men did not kneel to other men; even a client before a patron kept his feet. Arabs from the tribal towns are reported to have found the posture the hardest single thing about the new worship, and some negotiated over it. The ayah names it as the first and instinctive response of belief.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah carries one of the recitation marks that call for a prostration, and the surah takes its name from it. In the standard Uthmani text there are fifteen such marks in all, spread across surahs from the seventh to the ninety-sixth. This is the only one in this surah, and it falls almost exactly at its midpoint.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates faith in reaction rather than in assent. Someone who has to be argued into agreement each time is not described here at all; what is described is a person for whom the reminder does the work by itself. Pride is then identified as the specific obstacle, which places unbelief in the will rather than in the intellect and explains why more evidence is not always the remedy.

crossReferences.why: Describes those given knowledge earlier falling on their faces when the recitation is read to them.
Names prophets who fell prostrate and weeping when the signs of the Merciful were recited.
Closes a surah with those near God prostrating without arrogance, the same pairing as here.

studies.applyIt: The next time something you read or hear strikes you as true, notice how long the gap is before you start assessing it. This ayah describes people with almost no gap at all. You do not have to manufacture that. But you can watch for the moment you begin arguing with something you already know, and let it pass once.

studies.title: Their Sides Leave Their Beds
studies.meaning: The description begins with a body rather than with a state of mind. Their sides come away from the bedding, and the verb means to hold apart, so the picture is of a person lifting off the ground while the bed is still warm. Two motives are then named together and neither is corrected by the other: fear, and an eager wanting. The sentence does not stop there. It runs straight on into spending from what they were given, so the night hours and the open hand belong to one description.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah sets two responses to the same signs beside each other: those who go down in prostration when reminded, and those who turn away and are described immediately before this. Night prayer was practised in the community from early in Mecca, in houses rather than in public, and the commentators connect this ayah with that practice generally rather than reporting a particular occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: A verb of separation with an effort in it, used of two things that do not sit flush. It describes the gap opening between a body and the bedding rather than the act of standing up.
The plural of a place where one lies down on a side. It names the spot rather than the furniture, which fits a household where sleeping meant a mat or a folded cloak on the floor.
A word that elsewhere carries greed. Set beside fear as a motive for prayer, it describes wanting with appetite in it, not a mild or dutiful expectation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses were small and rooms were shared. Bedding was a mat or a cloak laid on a floor, and getting up in the middle of the night was heard by everyone lying nearby. Desert nights were cold, lamp oil cost money, and there was nothing to do in the dark that anyone could not account for. A person who rose regularly was known in their household to be rising.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah takes its name from the ayah immediately before this one, where those who believe fall down in prostration when the signs are recalled to them. It is one of the places in the Quran that the recitation tradition marks with a prostration, so the surah is named for a movement that readers still make when they reach it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear and hope are stated in the same clause without either being subordinated, which is how the classical tradition generally describes a heart in balance. The passage then joins private hours to public generosity in one sentence. What is done unseen at night and what is handed over in daylight are not offered as two virtues to be weighed against each other but as one continuous account of the same people.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same people from outside: little sleep taken, and asking forgiveness in the last dark hours.
Addresses the night vigil directly as something added on top of what is already kept.
Draws the contrast this passage assumes, between one devout through the night and one who is not.

studies.applyIt: Set your alarm ten minutes earlier than usual tomorrow and spend those ten minutes before you touch a screen. Sit up, say something, and let it be short. The ayah describes a gap opening between a body and a bed, and ten minutes is enough to find out what it costs you and what, if anything, it changes.

studies.title: What No Soul Knows
studies.meaning: The reward is described by refusing to describe it. No soul knows what has been kept hidden for them, which withholds precisely the thing a listener wants. A question follows that reads as rhetorical and is doing structural work, setting a person of faith beside one who has broken out of it and saying the two are not level. Then the destination is named with the word for food and lodging laid out for a guest who has just arrived, so the Garden is a reception rather than a settlement of accounts.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These lines answer the description just before them of people who rise at night and give from what they have. The community in Mecca was being told that what it was enduring had a counterpart, without being told what the counterpart consisted of. In a situation where nothing visible was on offer, the deliberate withholding is part of what is being said rather than a gap in the account.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb of concealment, with the agent unnamed. The hiding is presented as something done deliberately and kept, not as information that merely happens to be unavailable.
What a host sets out immediately for an arriving guest, before anything else is arranged. It names a first course rather than a final payment, which changes what the whole promise is.
A place one withdraws to for safety, used of where a traveller takes cover. Attached to gardens, it makes the destination a place of coming in from something rather than a prize.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality was the strongest obligation in that society. A traveller reaching a tent was fed from the best available before he was asked his name or his business, and a household that failed a guest carried the shame for a generation. The word used here for the reception is the one for that first provision set out at the door, so the Garden arrives in the vocabulary everyone already used for welcome.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical tradition preserves a divine saying that the commentators quote when they reach this ayah: that God has prepared for His righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The report is cited precisely because the ayah itself declines to fill in the picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is placed on description. What is promised is put beyond the reach of imagination, so the motive being offered is not a picture to be desired but confidence in the one making the offer. The word for hospitality then reframes the exchange: deeds are named as the occasion for a welcome rather than as its purchase price, which keeps the relationship from being read as a transaction.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for hospitality, with the gardens set out as a reception for those who arrive.
Puts the logic of the middle ayah as a question: is the reward for good anything other than good?
Shows the alternative approach, describing the reception in physical detail rather than withholding it.

studies.applyIt: Prepare one thing for a visitor before they arrive this week rather than after they sit down: the room aired, water poured, the thing they like already out. Do it for someone ordinary, not for a guest you are trying to impress. The word this passage uses for the Garden is the word for exactly that gesture.

studies.title: Every Time They Try To Leave
studies.meaning: The second half of a pair is given here, answering the shelter promised a moment earlier to those who believed. The same word is used for both destinations, so the contrast is exact: one shelter and another. What is added is repetition, an attempt to get out that is met each time by return, and words spoken to them naming what they had denied. The commentators note that the sentence closes on denial rather than on any other wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing a comparison the surah opened two ayat earlier by asking whether a believer and a transgressor could be equal. The surrounding argument has been about the reckoning that follows from God's government of the world. Commentators report no particular occasion and treat the passage as the answer to the surah's own rhetorical question, given in two matched halves rather than one.

keyTerms.note: The root describes a date stone slipping out of its fruit, or a creature leaving its shell. It names departure from something one belonged inside, which is why it is set opposite belief rather than opposite obedience.
The word for a place one comes home to at nightfall. Using it of the Fire is deliberate, since the previous ayah used the same word of the gardens, and the parallel is meant to be heard.
The imperative of tasting, used across the Quran for punishment. It names knowledge acquired by contact rather than by report, which answers precisely the kind of denial the ayah ends on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shelter carried a specific weight in a country where night in the open could kill. A traveller's whole day was planned around reaching a settlement, a walled garden or a tent whose owner would take him in. Refuge was the thing you moved towards. Hearing the same word attached to a fire that returns you whenever you try to leave inverted the most reliable comfort in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah just before this one sets out the reward and this one the recompense, and both use the same noun for the destination, a place of shelter. The closing clauses then diverge: the garden is given for what they used to do, while the Fire is named for what they used to deny.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By ending on what they denied rather than on what they did, the passage keeps its account of accountability tied to truth rather than to conduct alone. The repeated attempt and return also says something about finality that no single statement could: the outcome is not a sentence being served but a condition that has closed. The matched vocabulary insists both outcomes are of the same kind.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost the same picture of being returned whenever they try to escape from grief.
Asks the question this ayah completes: whether the faithful and the transgressor are equal.
States the same asymmetry flatly, that the two companies are not to be reckoned alike.

studies.applyIt: Notice the word this ayah uses twice, shelter, once for the garden and once for the Fire. Both are places people end up rather than places they suddenly arrive at. Ask yourself tonight what you have been drifting towards for the last year, without deciding anything about it. Naming the direction is the whole exercise.

studies.title: The Lesser Before The Greater
studies.meaning: A smaller affliction is described as coming first, ahead of a larger one, and a purpose is attached: so that they may return. The commentators differ over what the lesser refers to, offering the hardships of this life, the drought and hunger that struck Mecca, the losses of battle, and the pressure of the grave. None of them treat it as an instalment of the greater. The second ayah then names the wrong being answered, which is turning away after being reminded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to people who had heard the message repeatedly and set it aside. The commentators who read the lesser affliction as the famine that struck Mecca connect it to a period of severe shortage reported during the Meccan years, though the identification is one reading among several rather than an agreed occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A word that means both closer in distance and lower in degree. Both senses are active here: this affliction is nearer in time and smaller in scale than the one it comes before.
The ordinary verb for going back to a place you came from. Used of repentance, it treats turning to God as a return to something already left rather than as arrival somewhere new.
Built from the word for a side. To turn away in this sense is to present your flank, showing not disagreement but refusal to face, which is why it is named as worse than argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no farmland and lived on trade and imported grain, so a bad season anywhere along the caravan routes was felt immediately in its markets. Hunger there was a matter of prices and blocked roads rather than failed harvests. Everyone understood the difference between a hard year, which could be survived, and ruin, which could not. The ayah is speaking in that register of graded misfortune.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered here as the lesser torment occurs exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah, and its counterpart the greater torment is what it is set against. Because the expression appears nowhere else to clarify it, the classical commentators had only the context to work from, which is why they record a range of readings instead of one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assigns a purpose to affliction without claiming that every affliction has that purpose, and the difference matters for anyone reading it while suffering. What is described is a summons rather than an instalment of punishment, aimed at return. Set beside the second ayah, it also implies that the reminder itself is the first mercy, and that hardship follows only where the reminder has already been shown the flank.

crossReferences.why: Describes hardship sent to earlier communities with the same stated purpose, that they might humble themselves.
Says corruption appears so that God may let people taste part of what they did, that they return.
Names the same wrong of being reminded of God's signs and turning away from them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small thing that went wrong for you recently, too small to call a trial. Instead of asking why it happened, ask what it interrupted. Sometimes a minor disruption is the only thing that gets a person to look up from what they were doing. Give it five minutes today and see what you were in the middle of.

studies.title: Do Not Be In Doubt
studies.meaning: Three statements are compressed into one line: a Book was given to Moses, the hearer is told not to doubt a meeting, and that Book was made a guidance for the Children of Israel. The middle clause is the difficult one. The pronoun is open, and the classical commentators divide over whether the meeting is Moses receiving his Lord, the Prophet encountering Moses, or the meeting with God that awaits everyone. They record the range without forcing a choice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the point where the surah turns from argument to precedent. Having described revelation, denial and reckoning, it names an earlier instance of exactly that sequence. Commentators read the mention of Moses here as reassurance during a period of sustained rejection in Mecca: a Book had been given before, met with the same resistance, and had still become a guidance for a whole people.

keyTerms.note: A different word from the one used at the surah's opening. This one suggests contention and going back and forth over something, doubt that argues with itself rather than doubt that simply lacks information.

A noun of meeting whose possessive pronoun is grammatically open. The classical commentators record several readings of whose meeting is meant and treat the ambiguity as genuine rather than as something to be resolved.
The word is indefinite and stands as the whole predicate, so the Book is not said to contain guidance but to be it. The same construction opens the second surah of the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories of Moses circulated in Arabia well beyond the Jewish settlements of the north and of Yathrib. Traders returning from Syria carried them, and poets used their imagery. Meccan listeners did not need the narrative explained; they knew there had been a lawgiver with a book and a pursuing king. The surah can therefore invoke him in a single clause and rely on the whole account being present to its audience.
studies.didYouKnow: Moses is named more often in the Quran than any other person, appearing in over a hundred ayat spread across more than thirty surahs. This is one of his briefest mentions, a single clause with no narrative attached. The classical commentators treat such compressed references as written for an audience already holding the longer accounts given elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing this Book beside the earlier one establishes continuity rather than novelty, which was the contested point. Revelation is presented as a repeated act with a consistent pattern, so rejection in the present is neither unprecedented nor decisive. The open pronoun also leaves the reader with a question rather than a settled reading, and the tradition's willingness to leave it open is itself a lesson in how the text is handled.

crossReferences.why: Repeats that the Book of Moses was disputed, and links that dispute to this one.
Describes the same Book given to Moses as complete, a clear explanation and a mercy.
Names the Book given to Moses as guidance for the Children of Israel in nearly identical words.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the commentators on this ayah could not agree whose meeting is meant, and wrote that down instead of picking one. Try that once this week on something you have been asked about and do not actually know. Say you are not sure, and say what the possibilities are. It is a harder sentence to speak than it looks.

studies.title: As Long As They Persevered
studies.meaning: Leadership is described as something appointed rather than seized, and two conditions are attached to it: they persevered, and they held their certainty about God's signs. The commentators note the clause is temporal, so the guiding continues while the two conditions hold. The following ayah then removes the question of who was right from human hands entirely, assigning the settlement of every disputed matter to the Day of Resurrection rather than to any argument won in the meantime.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing the reference to Moses and the Children of Israel from the previous ayah. The commentators read the pairing as instruction for a small and pressed community: the earlier people were given leaders on terms, and those terms were endurance and conviction rather than numbers or power. The mention of disputes settled later addresses divisions among the earlier community that were well known to the audience.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the root for a road ahead or a pattern to be followed. It names people others take their direction from, and the ayah makes that position something given rather than claimed.
The root joins patience to restraint and to binding something in place. It covers holding a position under pressure as much as bearing pain, which is the sense the leadership clause needs.

A present tense inside a past narrative, so the certainty is described as continuous rather than as a moment. Paired with perseverance, it makes conviction a state that has to be held rather than reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leadership among the Arabs was not inherited cleanly. A chief held his position by consent that could be withdrawn, and his standing rested on judgement, generosity and the ability to absorb insult without losing authority. Everyone listening knew that men rose and fell in these assemblies by their conduct under pressure. The conditions this ayah attaches to leadership were therefore recognisable rather than abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for leaders occurs a small number of times in the Quran and is applied both to those who guide by God's command and, elsewhere in almost identical phrasing, to leaders who call towards the Fire. The classical commentators point out that the term itself is neutral and takes its whole value from the clause attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once. Guidance for others is treated as an appointment, not an achievement, which removes the claim from anyone who wants to assert it about himself. And the settling of disputes is postponed to a day when God does it, which limits how much any disagreement in this life can be closed. The community is asked to persevere without expecting the argument to end.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase of leaders appointed to guide by God's command among the prophets.
Applies the same word to leaders who call towards the Fire, showing the term's neutrality.
Also defers a disputed matter to the Day of Resurrection rather than settling it now.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you have been carrying that will not resolve, where you are fairly sure you are right. This passage does not ask you to concede it. It asks you to stop needing it closed. Set it down for a week without conceding anything, and notice how much energy you get back from not needing the verdict now.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: In Whose Dwellings They Walk
studies.meaning: The argument here is made of geography rather than words. Generations were destroyed, and the people being addressed live among what those generations built and walk through their houses. The evidence is under their feet daily. The closing question asks whether they hear, not whether they see, which the commentators find pointed: the ruins are visible to everyone, so the failure being named is in the reception rather than in the availability of the sign.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The trade routes north and south from Mecca ran past abandoned settlements, and the surrounding passages return repeatedly to earlier peoples who rejected messengers. Commentators identify the ruins generally rather than naming one site, since several were known to the caravans. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah is part of the surah's closing sequence of signs offered to people who had asked for one.

keyTerms.note: The word means both a span of time and the people who filled it, so a generation and its era are named by one term. It lets the ayah speak of vanished periods and vanished populations together.

From the root for stillness and settling down. A dwelling in this vocabulary is where motion stops, which sharpens the picture of later travellers moving through places built by people who had come to rest.

The verb of hearing where sight might be expected, since the ruins are looked at rather than listened to. Commentators read it as hearing with acceptance, the reception a report requires to do anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Northern Arabia was full of abandoned building. Rock-cut facades stood along the Syrian road, and the traces of older irrigation and settlement lay near the wells. Caravans camped in such places because they had water, so Meccan traders slept among ruins several times a year. The ayah does not describe something exotic. It describes an ordinary night's stop on a familiar route.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about walking through the dwellings of destroyed generations appears in more than one surah of this period, always offered as evidence rather than as narrative. Elsewhere the same argument is put in the second person, telling the listeners directly that they had lived in the homes of people who wronged themselves. The commentators treat the repetition as a settled form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Signs are described as failing at the point of reception rather than the point of delivery. What these listeners lack is not access, since they are physically standing inside the evidence, but the disposition that lets evidence register. That distinction runs through the surah, and it explains why the answer to demands for a further sign is so often another statement of what is already there.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same argument in nearly identical words and ends on those of understanding.
Names two earlier peoples whose ruined dwellings had already become plain to the listeners.
Tells the listeners they lived in the homes of those who wronged themselves, and were shown how.

studies.applyIt: Find one old thing on your ordinary route, a closed shop, a building older than you, a name on a stone. Stop at it once this week for a minute. The point is not sadness. It is that this passage treats a familiar object you walk past without noticing as an argument, and the noticing is the part it asks for.

studies.title: Water Driven To Barren Ground
studies.meaning: The verb chosen for the water is one used of driving animals, so the rain is described as herded to a place rather than falling on it. What grows there feeds livestock and people, in that order, which keeps the sign at the level of a meal rather than a spectacle. Then the objectors change the subject and ask when the promised outcome will arrive. The two ayat are placed together so the demand follows immediately on evidence already given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Rain in that country was local and unpredictable, arriving as a storm over one valley while the next stayed dry, and the sign would have been read against that experience. The demand in the second ayah belongs to the running Meccan dispute over a promised reckoning. Commentators note that similar demands are recorded across this period without any single occasion being attached to this one.

keyTerms.note: The verb for driving a herd along a route. Applied to water it makes rainfall a matter of direction and delivery rather than of chance distribution, which is the whole force of the image.
Land that has been cut back to nothing, with the vegetation gone rather than merely dormant. The word rules out the reading that the growth was already there and only needed watering.
A noun from the verb for opening, used of a judgement handed down and of a conquest. Commentators differ over which sense the objectors intended and which the answer takes up.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In the Hijaz a wadi could be bone dry for a year and then carry a torrent for an afternoon, and men who had learned where such flows arrived planted at those spots. Whole settlements existed because water had a habit of reaching one place. The picture of water conducted to a particular stretch of dead ground was therefore agricultural common sense before it was an argument about God.
studies.didYouKnow: The question asked in the second ayah, when is this opening, occurs in this exact form only once in the Quran. The classical commentators record three readings of what the objectors meant by it: the judgement of the Last Day, a decisive victory over them, or the conquest of Mecca. They report the range without settling on one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing is doing an argumentative job. A sign is offered that repeats every year and requires nothing to be taken on trust, and the response is a demand for a different and larger sign. That sequence is the surah's standing account of unbelief: not a shortage of evidence but an appetite for evidence of a kind that would end the possibility of choosing, which is precisely what is withheld.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same driving of clouds to dead land and calls the result the resurrection.
Describes blessed water sent down and gardens raised, ending on the coming forth.
Shows those who do not believe in the Hour demanding its arrival in the same tone.

studies.applyIt: Drink a glass of water today and follow it backwards in your mind, to the tap, the pipe, the reservoir, the cloud. Take twenty seconds over it. This ayah is not asking for awe at something rare. It is asking you to give the same attention to an ordinary supply that you would give a miracle you had demanded.

studies.title: Turn Away And Wait
studies.meaning: The demand made a moment earlier is answered without giving a date. What is described instead is the shape of the day when it comes: belief declared then will not help, and no interval will be granted for anything to be put right. The surah then closes by telling the Prophet to turn away and wait, and adds that his opponents are waiting too. Both parties are left in the same posture, and only the object of their waiting differs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the final two ayat of the surah. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was under sustained ridicule in Mecca with no visible change in his situation, and the instruction to withdraw and wait belongs to that period. Commentators note that surahs of these years often close on a command to endure rather than on a resolution, which matches the community's circumstances at the time.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the root for looking, which in this form means to be granted a delay. The same root gives the word for waiting used at the end, so the two ayat are joined by one family of meaning.

The same verb used earlier in the surah of those who turned from God's signs, now given as an instruction. Commentators read it as ceasing to press an argument rather than as abandoning the people themselves.
A participle describing a settled state rather than an action. Applied to both sides, it says the two groups are doing the same thing and differ only in what they expect to arrive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting was ordinary work in that economy. A caravan sent north was gone for months, and the families behind it lived on an outcome they could not influence and could not hurry. Merchants spoke of ventures as things that would come back or would not. The last word of this surah puts the Prophet and his opponents into that familiar posture, two parties with capital committed and no way to speed the return.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of the surah comes from the same root as the reprieve denied in the ayah just before it, so the closing waiting and the refused delay are relatives in Arabic. Several surahs of this period end on a similar instruction to wait, and the classical commentators treat the pattern as characteristic of the Meccan years.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the value of belief depend partly on when it is offered, which is a hard claim and stated plainly. It also equalises the two sides in an unexpected way: waiting is not a defeat but the shared condition of everyone before an outcome nobody controls. Confidence is located in what is expected rather than in how the wait feels, which is the whole difference between the parties.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule, that faith declared once the punishment is seen will not benefit.
Says belief will not help a soul that did not believe before certain signs arrive.
Ends with the same instruction to wait, and says the speaker waits alongside them.

studies.applyIt: There is something you are waiting on that has no date attached. Notice that this surah ends by telling its reader to wait, and does not soften it with an estimate. Try naming your own wait out loud once today, plainly, without adding a guess about how long. Waiting well starts with admitting that is what you are doing.
